title: The Fall of Jerusalem
overview: Babylon besieges and destroys Jerusalem and its temple, most of the people are taken into exile, and the book ends with a captive king of Judah being shown kindness in Babylon.

parts.label: Siege and Zedekiah's capture (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: Zedekiah had sworn loyalty to Babylon and then rebelled, so Babylon surrounded Jerusalem for about two years until the people starved and the wall was broken through. His sons were killed in front of him and he was blinded, a brutal punishment for breaking his oath that also ended any chance of him or his heirs ruling again.

parts.label: City and temple burned (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: About a month later, Babylon's commander burned the temple, the palace and the city's houses and tore down the walls. Most of the remaining people were taken away as captives, and only the poorest were left to farm the land.

parts.label: Temple treasures carried off (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: The great bronze pillars, the stands and the huge bronze basin called the Sea, all made in Solomon's day, were broken up and hauled to Babylon as metal. The detailed description recalls how large and richly decorated Solomon's temple had been.

parts.label: Leaders executed (vv. 18-21)
parts.note: The king of Babylon had the chief priests, senior temple officials, an army commander and royal advisers put to death, probably treating them as responsible for the revolt. The closing summary, that Judah was taken from its land, marks the end of the kingdom as an independent nation.

parts.label: Gedaliah's short rule (vv. 22-26)
parts.note: Babylon made Gedaliah, whose father had protected the prophet Jeremiah, governor of those left behind, and he urged them to accept Babylon's rule and settle down. Ishmael, a member of the royal family, murdered him, and the survivors fled to Egypt, afraid Babylon would punish them all.

parts.label: Jehoiachin freed (vv. 27-30)
parts.note: Thirty-seven years after he was taken captive, the former king Jehoiachin was released by a new Babylonian king and given honor and daily food for the rest of his life. Christians later read this in light of the fact that Jehoiachin appears in Jesus' family line in Matthew's Gospel, as a sign that David's royal line was not cut off.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the closing release of Jehoiachin is meant as a quiet sign of hope that David's royal line would continue, or simply as a final note confirming that the kingdom was over.
think: When the things a people built their identity around are destroyed, what do you think makes it possible for them to keep going, or makes it impossible?
